$700 million investment includes rights to distribute Cornerstone Robotics' Sentire™ surgical system in select markets outside the U.S.

Sentire will be a strong complement to Medtronic's Hugo™ robotic-assisted surgery (RAS) system, creating a unique portfolio of robotic solutions

GALWAY, Ireland, Sept. 1, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Medtronic, a global leader in healthcare technology, today announced a strategic partnership with Cornerstone Robotics, an innovative surgical robotics company committed to advancing minimally invasive surgery and improving access to the latest surgical care worldwide. The approximately $700 million investment includes rights to distribute Cornerstone Robotics' Sentire™ surgical system in select markets outside the U.S. where the system is market approved.

Medtronic will distribute Sentire alongside its Hugo™ robotic-assisted surgery (RAS) system. Together with Medtronic's connected surgical ecosystem, the two complementary platforms will expand access to robotic-assisted surgery and offer surgeons and health systems more choice and flexible solutions designed to meet their diverse needs and reach more patients globally.

With global adoption of robotic-assisted surgery still in the single digits, the opportunity to expand access to advanced surgical care for patients, physicians and health systems around the world is significant. Expanded choice and access are critical drivers of the future of robotic assisted surgery. Through this partnership, Medtronic and Cornerstone Robotics are building a multi-port portfolio anchored by the Hugo RAS system and expanded by Sentire, giving customers meaningful flexibility across clinical settings, procedural needs, and economic models.

"Our strategy is focused on driving the next generation of minimally invasive surgery, one of our biggest growth opportunities," said Matt Anderson, senior vice president and president, Surgical, Medtronic. "Surgeons, health systems and markets have varying needs and preferences, which is why we are investing across robotic platforms, digital tools and platform-enhancing technologies. With Sentire complementing the Hugo RAS system, Medtronic will be the only company offering this two-platform portfolio combined with our surgical ecosystem—giving customers more access, more choice, and flexible solutions that fit their clinical and operational needs."

Building on Hugo's momentum

The partnership builds on the momentum of Medtronic's Hugo RAS system, which is now being used in more than 35 countries across six continents, including the United States, where it received FDA clearance within the last year. Procedure growth for the Hugo RAS system is currently more than two times the growth rate of the robotic surgery market, and total procedures are expected to exceed 50,000 globally by the end of Medtronic's fiscal year.

Medtronic will continue to innovate the capabilities of the Hugo RAS system, including ongoing software upgrades, real-time artificial intelligence across its digital ecosystem, integrated stapling, expanded instrumentation, and clinical indications. The modular, multi-quadrant platform is designed for a broad range of soft-tissue surgical procedures and combines wristed instruments, 3D visualization, and Touch Surgery™ ecosystem with dedicated support for robotics program optimization, service, and training.

Expanding Access Through Sentire Surgical System

The Sentire system's architecture and immersive console with dual-console capability offer a familiar configuration suited to varying surgeon preferences and clinical needs. Developed entirely in-house by Cornerstone Robotics, Sentire has completed multi-specialty clinical trials and received CE Mark in May 2026 for use in minimally invasive general, gynecologic, thoracic, and urologic surgical procedures in addition to its market approval in China and Singapore.

"Since the founding of Cornerstone Robotics, we have been steadfast in our commitment to innovation, excellence and clinical value," said Samuel Au, founder and CEO, Cornerstone Robotics. "We are confident physicians and patients alike will be the greatest beneficiaries of this partnership as we continue to expand access across this dynamic market."

Medtronic continues to invest across its surgical ecosystem to expand access to robotic-assisted solutions for operating rooms around the world. This partnership is another step in strengthening that connected ecosystem and advancing the company's commitment to improving the lives of patients through minimally invasive surgery.

text:
GALWAY, Ireland and REHOVOT, Israel, Sept. 1, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Medtronic plc (NYSE: MDT), a global leader in healthcare technology, and Pi-Cardia Ltd., a pioneer in leaflet modification technologies for structural heart disease, today announced a strategic investment by Medtronic in Pi-Cardia Ltd. With a focus on addressing the evolving needs of increasingly complex transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) patients and procedures, Medtronic secures an option for strengthening its structural heart portfolio through this strategic investment, supporting the next generation of innovation.

Pi-Cardia's ShortCut™ device is the first FDA-cleared leaflet modification technology designed to enable valve-in-valve TAVR procedures in patients at risk of coronary obstruction. The device provides physicians with a safe, easy-to-learn, reproducible approach to leaflet modification that can help preserve coronary access and enable future transcatheter valve procedures. In FDA-reviewed clinical studies, ShortCut™ demonstrated successful leaflet splitting in all pivotal trial patients and a favorable safety profile.

"As structural heart care evolves, we're investing in technologies that help physicians address today's challenges while preparing for tomorrow's opportunities," said Jorie Soskin, vice president and general manager of the Structural Heart business within Medtronic's Cardiovascular portfolio. "Our investment in Pi-Cardia reflects our commitment to building a portfolio of technologies that will shape the future of TAVR, particularly for patients with complex anatomy. We believe leaflet modification technologies like ShortCut have the potential to become an important component of structural heart care and the future of TAVR as transcatheter therapies continue to advance."

Under the agreement, Medtronic will make strategic investments of up to $80 million into Pi-Cardia and is expected to become the exclusive global commercial distributor of the ShortCut device in 2027. Medtronic will leverage its worldwide Structural Heart organization to expand physician access across the United States, Europe, Japan and other international markets. The agreement also includes an option for Medtronic to acquire Pi-Cardia upon achievement of predefined milestones for an estimated upfront acquisition price of up to $210 million, subject to customary adjustments, plus additional potential earn-out payments post-acquisition that could meaningfully increase the total consideration. The transactions are subject to regulatory approval and customary closing conditions.

"Our mission has been to make leaflet modification a standard part of complex TAVR," said Erez Golan, Chief Executive Officer of Pi-Cardia. "Medtronic is the right partner to help us achieve this vision given their global reach and commitment to bringing innovative tools to physicians and patients worldwide. We are confident this collaboration will accelerate adoption of ShortCut while continuing to advance the future of leaflet modification."

The strategic investment secures an option for Medtronic to strengthen its structural heart portfolio by adding a first-of-its-kind technology that addresses a significant challenge in valve-in-valve TAVR while complementing the company's leadership in transcatheter valve therapies. It also reflects Medtronic's commitment to partnering and investing early in innovations that can improve patient outcomes, expand future treatment options, and support long-term growth.

Pi-Cardia was founded by Erez Golan and Eyal Kolka, and is backed by experienced medtech investors including Sofinnova Partners, Sprig Equity, and Jacques Séguin, whose commitment has helped advance the company's vision of developing transformative leaflet modification technologies.

name: L’Oréal
title: Why luxury beauty giants are betting big on India
description:
Luxury beauty giants are no longer treating India as an emerging market.
Long before global beauty giants began looking towards the country, Indian consumers were already experimenting, adapting and creating their own rituals.
The lipstick economy outpacing the luxury wardrobe Luxury beauty is growing faster than categories like watches, jewelry, fashion, and cars, driven by affluent consumers and stronger trust in locally available luxury brands.
Customers who previously traveled abroad for luxury beauty can now confidently buy these products domestically because of brand credibility and partner support.
It’s a reminder that Indian ingredients have been shaping global luxury beauty for generations.” says Diipa.
text:
Luxury beauty giants are no longer treating India as an emerging market. Major acquisitions, entry markets, flagship boutiques, omnichannel expansion and creator-led storytelling are all proof that global players are racing to secure a place in one of the world’s deepest mines for the fastest-growing prestige beauty markets.

Every Indian girl knows the image. Aishwarya Rai Bachchan, ethereal and luminous, gliding through a L’Oréal Paris campaign with silk-like, impossibly lustrous hair, saying “Because you’re worth it” (before most of us even knew what a serum was). A Dior lipstick picked up on a trip to Paris or dousing yourself in a bottle of Chanel No. 5 perched on a vanity or at duty free.

French pharmacy shelves overflowing with cult skincare that somehow felt more magical because “it came from France”. For decades, French beauty wasn’t merely a category, it was the passport to luxury, discovered through glossy campaigns and souvenirs carried home in shopping bags long before they arrived on Indian shelves. Today, the gaze has shifted. France has its eyes on India.

France occupies a unique position within prestige beauty. Home to L’Oréal, LVMH, Kering Beauté, Chanel, Dior, Guerlain, Sisley and countless heritage fragrance maisons, the country has spent decades shaping the codes of luxury beauty. For Indian consumers, French beauty has long represented craftsmanship, science, heritage and aspiration in equal measure.

“I remember being a teenager and using kajal to give myself winged eyeliner because I saw it in a magazine,” Diipa Khosla

India’s relationship with beauty has always been a conversation between tradition and transformation. Long before global beauty giants began looking towards the country, Indian consumers were already experimenting, adapting and creating their own rituals.

Today, consumers discover a product on TikTok, Instagram or Paris Fashion Week and expect to find it on Indian shelves almost immediately. They no longer ask if a brand is available in India. They ask why it isn’t yet.

Every luxury market has its gateway purchase. For some, it’s a silk scarf. For others, a Swiss watch or an Italian handbag. But for millions of consumers, luxury begins with something far more intimate: the swipe of a Dior Lip Addict lip oil, their first Chanel lipstick, the spritz of a YSL perfume they’ve seen on every banner, or the ritual of an overpriced serum before bed.

French beauty has long been a democratic dream, offering consumers their first taste of luxury, heritage, and prestige long before couture ever enters the picture. What is interesting is that India is no longer simply buying French beauty. It is becoming one of the markets shaping its future. But, can India remain a prestige market without becoming over-discounted?

Why every global beauty giant wants a piece of India

According to NielsenIQ’s India’s Beauty Moment: Growth, Shifts & Strategies for 2026, India is now among the world’s fastest growing beauty markets, with beauty outperforming adjacent consumer categories through sustained double-digit growth.

The report identifies premiumization, omnichannel retail, digital first brands and social commerce as the forces redefining the industry, while the convergence of beauty and wellness continues to reshape how consumers shop, spend and engage with prestige brands.

Globally, online beauty sales are growing six times faster than in store sales, making omnichannel no longer an advantage but an expectation. Meanwhile, 52 per cent of consumers are willing to pay a premium for convenience, while 49 per cent are willing to spend more on locally made products, signaling a customer who values both global prestige and local relevance. Luxury today is measured by accessibility, immediacy, and trust.

Roshan Kunder, Marketing Head, Bioderma India, says the country’s rapidly growing premium beauty ecosystem is being fueled by increasingly informed consumers who are prioritizing science backed skincare and skin health. As awareness grows, brands are investing not only in distribution but also in consumer education, dermatologist partnerships and long-term accessibility across both online and offline retail.

The lipstick economy outpacing the luxury wardrobe

Luxury beauty is growing faster than categories like watches, jewelry, fashion, and cars, driven by affluent consumers and stronger trust in locally available luxury brands. Customers who previously traveled abroad for luxury beauty can now confidently buy these products domestically because of brand credibility and partner support.

“We also look at watches, jewellery, fashion, cars, all of these categories, but when you look at how they’re all growing, it’s actually beauty which is the one that’s thriving the most, and double digit growth: upwards of 25% depending on which year you look at it, and we expect it to continue to grow. Why? Because we know that there’s more and more affluent consumers out in the market who are ready to spend that money, but also because there’s increasing confidence in what we as brands can offer to the consumer.

A lot of these customers were traveling abroad to buy their luxury beauty, now they can get it here, and they can trust the brands, and they can trust the brands because of the work that we do with you. They can understand that we are bringing the brands here because worldwide have authority. You give them faith to be able to buy those products here and experience those brands here.” Shreshta Jana Director – Luxury Division, L’Oréal India

If handbags announce wealth, beauty quietly reveals aspiration. It is often the first luxury purchase; the category consumers return to most frequently and, increasingly, the one rewriting the rules of global luxury growth.

“The response since our debut has exceeded expectations and reinforced India’s importance as a strategic market for Shiseido in Asia Pacific. With strong consumer demand and a clear connection to the brand, this is the right moment to deepen NARS’ retail presence.” Sanjay Sharma, Country Head, Shiseido India

Since entering India in 2023, NARS has seen stronger-than-expected demand, giving the brand confidence to expand its retail footprint. Sanjay Sharma says the focus isn’t on opening stores quickly but on creating immersive spaces where consumers can experience the brand’s artistry, personalised services and global product lineup.

He believes today’s Indian beauty shopper is informed, discerning and increasingly willing to invest in premium products, particularly high-performance complexion makeup. Going forward, NARS plans to grow steadily across the right retail destinations while bringing Indian consumers closer to its global launches and signature beauty experiences.

India’s beauty consumer was always ahead of the conversation

“It has one of the youngest populations in the world, a rapidly growing premium beauty market, and consumers who are incredibly engaged. It’s grown into a market the world can learn from.” Diipa Khosla

What the industry is recognizing today is that the Indian consumer was never simply waiting to be introduced to beauty trends; they were already decoding, adapting and personalizing them.

Apart from this notion, the rise of the informed beauty consumer is one trend nearly every executive agrees on. According to Roshan Kunder, Marketing Head, Bioderma India, today’s luxury beauty customer is looking far beyond marketing claims, placing greater emphasis on ingredient transparency, scientific credibility and dermatologist backed formulations.

“Consumers are looking beyond trends and seeking products backed by science and proven efficacy,” he says, adding that skincare has become the foundation of the modern beauty journey, with purchasing decisions increasingly shaped by education, efficacy and long-term results rather than impulse alone.

From Shelf Space to Stakeholders

The confidence global beauty houses have in India is already translating into investment. Earlier this year, The Estée Lauder Companies completed its acquisition of the remaining stake in Forest Essentials in a deal valued at approximately $63 million, turning one of India’s most iconic Ayurvedic luxury beauty brands into a wholly owned part of its global portfolio.

Around the same time, reports suggested L’Oréal Group was evaluating an investment in Indian personal care company Innovist, reinforcing a broader shift taking place across the industry. The world’s largest beauty companies are no longer treating India simply as another retail destination. They are investing in its brands, its consumers, and its long-term potential. L’Oréal was approached for executive insights for this feature; however, the company declined to comment.

The next phase of luxury beauty growth will be won through accessibility rather than availability alone. Bioderma sees omnichannel retail as central to that strategy. According to Kunder, consumers now expect a seamless experience regardless of where they discover or purchase a product, making e commerce, premium beauty retailers and dermatology led consultation complementary rather than competing channels. The objective is no longer simply expanding shelf space but creating a consistent luxury experience across every touchpoint.

The momentum extends well beyond the boardrooms. Global maisons are accelerating retail expansion through partners including Shoppers Stop Beauty, Sephora, Nykaa Luxe, Tira and Tata CLiQ Luxury, while bringing international launches to India faster than ever before.

“Every boutique is a strategic building block in NARS’ India journey. We are expanding thoughtfully rather than growing simply for scale.” Sanjay Sharma

Dedicated India campaigns, local ambassadors, creator collaborations and immersive retail experiences are replacing the old model where prestige beauty arrived months after global launches. The dream once sold to Indian consumers through French campaigns has come full circle. Today, France isn’t just selling beauty to India, it’s betting a winning hand on India’s beautiful future.

Beauty minus the jet lag: does French beauty speak in Hindi?

“Even something like our ‘Tyla Baddies’ moment wasn’t really about one viral reel. It was a reflection of a much bigger cultural shift. Indian beauty didn’t suddenly become cool overnight, the rest of the world just started paying attention. And yes, it was a long time coming, but now that we’re here, I think it’s such an exciting place to be.”— Diipa Khosla

The Indian customer is deeply aware of global trends: when a product launches in the US or UK, demand starts here almost instantly. More trust, more access, and a consumer who knows exactly what they want, safe to say the future of luxury beauty in India looks stronger than ever.

Perhaps it is also a long overdue recognition of a culture that has always spoken its own language of beauty. We do not need to be considered “hot” by Western standards to deserve representation or to escape the racism that has long shaped global beauty ideals.

“Over the last few years, I’ve watched that change quite dramatically. I think people are becoming much more curious because social media has finally allowed them to see India through our eyes and not through the western gaze.” Diipa Khosla

From hidden ingredients to the bindi and kohl box

“When I first started creating content, I often felt like people had a very narrow idea of what Indian beauty looked like, we were often locked into a bindi & kohl box. There wasn’t much room for the version I knew growing up – one that was modern, ambitious, global, but still deeply connected to where it came from.” Diipa Khosla

India’s influence on global beauty is not new. Its ingredients, rituals and botanical knowledge have quietly shaped luxury beauty for generations. India is owning intellectual property and sharing its cultural context with the world.

“Indian beauty didn’t suddenly become cool overnight, the rest of the world just started paying attention. My favourite example is one I learnt while creating our own fragrances, and it’s about one of the most famous French fragrances of all time. It was originally formulated with sandalwood from Mysore, and although they have now switched to a synthetic alternative those vintage bottles are coveted for being richer and creamier with a softer, more complex dry-down than modern formulations because of the Sandalwood. It’s a reminder that Indian ingredients have been shaping global luxury beauty for generations.” says Diipa.

Sanjay Sharma evokes the same notion: “Indian consumers are expressive, well informed and increasingly willing to invest in high quality beauty. They expect products that perform, feel relevant and help them express their individuality.”

As luxury beauty becomes more crowded, heritage alone is no longer enough to command loyalty. “Consumers are looking beyond marketing claims and seeking brands backed by science, transparency and proven efficacy,” says Roshan Kunder, Marketing Head, Bioderma India. In a market flooded with launches, trust has quietly become luxury’s newest currency. The brands likely to win are not necessarily the loudest, but the ones that can consistently educate, perform, and build long term credibility.

What is satisfying is that a generation that once memorized French beauty campaigns is now quietly influencing the boardrooms that create them. India has moved from the waiting list to the priority list.

text:
Shares of MediaTek closed 10% higher on Tuesday after the Taiwanese chip firm announced a partnership with Nvidia , bolstering its push into the data center market.

Nvidia invested $3.5 billion in convertible bonds issued by MediaTek as part of the deal, the companies said on Monday, adding fuel to a near 200% rally in the Taiwanese firm's shares this year.

MediaTek is the world's biggest smartphone chip company by market share, according to Counterpoint Research, and the main rival to U.S. giant Qualcomm . But MediaTek has recently looked to diversify by designing custom chips for data centres.

Hyperscalers and other tech companies are increasingly building custom chips to run AI workloads. MediaTek is emerging as a player that can build these, posing a potential challenge to Broadcom , a market leader.

The partnership will see MediaTek offer Nvidia's NVLink Fusion platform for customers developing custom AI chips. That means the custom semiconductors that MediaTek builds can be integrated with Nvidia's AI infrastructure and systems.

NVLink Fusion is part of Nvidia's strategy to stay central to AI infrastructure even as companies move toward using their own chips to run certain AI processes.

The two companies will also work together on "local AI computing," which means chips designed for PCs as well as systems for cars.

In June, MediaTek said its custom AI chip business would bring in $2 billion of revenue this year with a total addressable market of up to $80 billion by 2027.

CNBC has reached out to MediaTek to ask if the Nvidia deal has changed that guidance.

In a press release issued on Monday, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang called MediaTek "one of the world's great semiconductor companies."

The two companies plan to work together on local AI computing and AI-powered vehicle platforms, while also bringing Nvidia's accelerated-computing technology into more markets.

The investment comes soon after Nvidia reported another strong quarter and projected roughly 70% revenue growth for fiscal 2028. That outlook suggests management still expects AI demand to grow rather than reach a peak. For NVDA investors, the key question is whether the MediaTek deal will create new demand for Nvidia's technology or is mainly another case of the company using its balance sheet to support the wider AI ecosystem.

Bull Case

The clearest positive is that the MediaTek partnership could expand NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA)'s addressable market beyond traditional data centers. MediaTek has a strong presence in smartphones, consumer electronics, connectivity and automotive chips. Pairing that reach with Nvidia's accelerated-computing technology could help Nvidia bring AI computing to edge devices, PCs and vehicles. The companies also launched the RTX Spark PC chip in June, showing that the relationship goes beyond a financial investment.

The automotive opportunity could be especially important. Nvidia is trying to make its technology a broader computing platform rather than remain mainly a supplier of data-center GPUs. Working with a major chip designer such as MediaTek could give Nvidia another path into AI-powered vehicles and other edge applications.

Investing through convertible bonds also gives Nvidia a strategic benefit. The company is not simply providing MediaTek with capital. It is building a closer financial relationship while potentially gaining equity exposure. If MediaTek's business grows as a result of the partnership, Nvidia could benefit financially while also seeing greater demand for its own technology.

More broadly, the deal fits NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA)'s strategy of building an ecosystem around its AI platform. The company has increasingly used investments, partnerships and financing arrangements to encourage customers and technology partners to expand AI infrastructure. Nvidia's equity investments had reached $99 billion as of July 26, with another $25 billion in commitments.

The strategy carries risks, but the bull case is fairly simple: if Nvidia can turn these ecosystem investments into significantly more demand for its chips and platforms, the returns could be much larger than the initial capital outlay.

Bear Case

The biggest concern is that NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) is increasingly financing the ecosystem that ultimately buys its products. The MediaTek investment is relatively small compared with Nvidia's overall resources, but it comes alongside much larger commitments elsewhere. Nvidia has already helped finance and support AI infrastructure projects, including arrangements connected to OpenAI. The company is increasingly taking on part of the working-capital burden of its own customer base.

That creates a potential circular-financing problem. NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) invests in companies or infrastructure projects; those businesses use the capital to expand AI capacity, and some of that spending can eventually flow back to Nvidia through purchases of its hardware.

That does not necessarily make the investments a bad decision. But investors still need to separate organic end-market demand from demand supported by Nvidia's own capital. There is also no guarantee that the MediaTek relationship will generate meaningful revenue for Nvidia anytime soon. AI PCs, edge AI and autonomous vehicles are large potential markets, but turning that potential into revenue could take years. The $3.5 billion investment should not be viewed as $3.5 billion of incremental Nvidia revenue.

Another risk is that Nvidia is committing capital while investors are already questioning the economics of the broader AI buildout. There are still concerns about the gap between huge AI infrastructure spending and the slower development of profitable AI applications.

Nvidia also faces growing competition from custom AI chips developed by its own customers and other semiconductor companies. Nvidia's broader accelerated-computing platform gives it an advantage over specialized chips, but the shift toward custom silicon remains a long-term risk to its pricing power and market share. Nvidia's financial commitments are also becoming large enough that investors may start looking for clear returns on invested capital instead of simply viewing each new partnership as a positive.

Conclusion

The MediaTek investment is strategically positive for NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA), especially because it could expand the company's reach into AI PCs, edge computing, and automobiles. MediaTek's customer base and chip-design expertise could give Nvidia a more efficient way to enter these markets.

The main risk is Nvidia's growing use of its own capital to support the AI ecosystem. If those investments lead to more demand for Nvidia's technology, they could generate strong long-term returns. If AI spending slows, the returns on those investments could be much weaker.

Overall, the deal adds to Nvidia's long-term growth story but is unlikely to have a major impact on near-term earnings. The bigger questions are whether AI demand remains strong, whether Nvidia can defend its competitive position, and whether its growing ecosystem investments generate attractive returns.

text:
The former French Minister for Labour and Employment joins AXA's top table just weeks after leaving parliament

Insurance News

By Josh Recamara

Sep 01, 2026 Share

AXA has appointed Astrid Panosyan-Bouvet (pictured) as group chief human resources officer and a member of its Management Committee, effective Sept. 1, 2026.

She will be responsible for all HR activities led at group level, including talent management, compensation, social relations, HR operations, culture and diversity, learning and development, and HR for AXA's headquarters, reporting to Karima Silvent, deputy general secretary.

The appointment is notable for the breadth of Panosyan-Bouvet's career, which spans corporate insurance, retail real estate, and, most recently, French national politics. She left the French National Assembly in August 2026, just weeks before joining AXA, having served as Minister for Labour and Employment from 2024 to 2025 under the Barnier and Bayrou governments.

A career that began at AXA and later returned to it

Panosyan-Bouvet's professional path started at AXA itself, where she worked as an M&A project manager between 1998 and 2001. She then moved into senior management roles at insurer Groupama from 2002 to 2014, followed by leadership positions at Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield from 2015 to 2022, during which she also served as a member of Air France-KLM's supervisory board.

Her career has also run through the French public sector. She advised the Ministry of the Economy, Industry and Digital Affairs on economic attractiveness and international investment between 2014 and 2015, was elected to the National Assembly for a Paris constituency in 2022, and was appointed Minister for Labour and Employment in September 2024. After leaving that post in December 2024, she was tasked by the prime minister with a mission on economic attractiveness before departing parliament entirely in August 2026.

Thomas Buberl, AXA's chief executive, said he was delighted to welcome Panosyan-Bouvet to the group and its Management Committee, adding that her extensive professional experience, knowledge of the industry, and strong convictions around culture, lifelong learning and diversity would be significant assets for AXA's next strategic plan.

Karima Silvent, to whom Panosyan-Bouvet will report, previously held the group HR director role herself before being promoted to deputy general secretary in October 2025, specifically as AXA began preparing its next strategic cycle. That sequencing means Panosyan-Bouvet's appointment fills a vacancy created by an internal promotion tied to strategic planning, rather than a departure or reshuffle prompted by performance concerns, and places her directly under someone who understands the HR function from the inside.

Beyond her corporate and political roles

Panosyan-Bouvet has also been active in the non-profit sector, having chaired the mentoring association Proxité on a voluntary basis between 2016 and 2019, and currently sits on the board of Forces Femmes, an organisation supporting women's economic reintegration. She is a graduate of Sciences Po Paris, HEC and Harvard's Kennedy School.

Appointing a former labour minister to lead HR is a distinctive choice for a company the size of AXA, and one that plausibly reflects a deliberate bet: someone who has recently sat on the other side of the table from employers, setting national labour policy, may bring a different lens to questions of workforce culture, social relations and talent strategy than a purely corporate HR background would.

Whether that translates into a meaningfully different approach at AXA specifically will likely become clearer once the group's next strategic plan, which Buberl explicitly linked to her appointment, takes shape.

description:

The benchmark combined multiple services and deployment models across Microsoft Azure, including Azure Kubernetes Service, Azure Container Apps, Azure SQL Database and Azure Database for PostgreSQL.

text:
It is no longer simply about how many transactions a core banking platform can process. Banks increasingly need to support transactions, real-time enquiries, payments, APIs, modular services and AI-powered interactions — often simultaneously.

The 2026 Temenos Highwater Benchmark on Microsoft Azure explored what this means at scale.

The benchmark tested Lending, Deposits Modularity, Temenos Payments Hub, Holdings and Party microservices and, for the first time within the benchmark transaction mix, Copilot for Core.

Testing was conducted against large-scale datasets, including 50 million customers and up to 125 million accounts. Overall throughput reached 16,385 transactions per second, including 12,241 TPS across Holdings enquiries, 2,109 TPS for Deposits, 1,539 TPS for Lending and 252 TPS for Copilot for Core. Temenos Payments Hub also processed 244 payment orders per second.

But the real story is not simply the headline number.

Three takeaways stand out.

1. Scale Is Now a Multi-Workload Challenge

The 2026 benchmark used a workload mix of 76.2% enquiries and 23.8% transactions, reflecting the increasingly diverse demands placed on modern banking platforms.

Customers check balances and transaction histories, digital channels continuously access APIs, employees retrieve information and payment services operate in real time — all while core transactions continue to be processed.

In the benchmark, balance enquiries reached 4,845 TPS with an average response time of 5 milliseconds, while transaction-list enquiries achieved 2,988 TPS at 6 milliseconds.

For banks, this changes the scalability question.

It is no longer simply:

“How fast is the core?”

It is increasingly:

“Can the entire banking architecture continue to perform predictably as the workload mix evolves?”

This means looking beyond transaction volumes to consider throughput, latency and resource utilisation across the wider banking platform.

2. Modularity Is Proving Its Value at Scale

A second important takeaway is the role of modular architecture.

The benchmark combined multiple services and deployment models across Microsoft Azure, including Azure Kubernetes Service, Azure Container Apps, Azure SQL Database and Azure Database for PostgreSQL. It also incorporated Arm-based Azure infrastructure, including Microsoft Cobalt technology, as part of the platform environment.

Deposits Modularity achieved 2,109 TPS, with the benchmark demonstrating near-linear scalability across vertical and horizontal scaling scenarios while meeting defined response-time requirements.

There were also notable year-on-year improvements within the microservices architecture.

Moving the Customer Enquiry API from Transact to the Party microservice resulted in an 82% improvement in response time, while database resource utilisation for Holdings was reduced by 57% during the mixed workload run.

For financial institutions, the significance goes beyond performance.

Modularity allows individual banking capabilities to evolve and scale according to their own workload requirements. This can support a more progressive approach to modernisation, enabling banks to evolve specific capabilities while remaining part of a coherent banking platform.

3. AI Is Becoming Part of the Banking Workload

Perhaps the most significant development in this year’s benchmark was the inclusion of Copilot for Core within the transaction mix for the first time.

Copilot for Core is an AI-powered assistant embedded in Temenos Core, designed to help bank users retrieve information through natural-language interactions and accelerate everyday operations.

During the benchmark, Copilot-related workloads achieved 252 TPS alongside traditional banking services.

This signals an important shift.

Much of the industry’s AI conversation has focused on use cases and productivity. But as AI becomes embedded into everyday banking operations, it also becomes an infrastructure and performance consideration.

AI services interact with data, consume compute and create demand alongside core banking, payments and other services.

For banks, this means AI increasingly needs to be considered not simply as an additional feature, but as part of the operational workload of the banking platform.

Building for What’s Next

The 2026 Highwater Benchmark points towards banking architectures that are becoming more modular, more distributed and more intelligent.

The broader takeaway for technology leaders is therefore more important than any individual TPS figure:

Design for the workload mix you expect tomorrow, not simply the transactions you process today.

That means preparing for transactions, enquiries, payments, modular services and AI-powered interactions to coexist and scale together.

Microsoft Azure provides the cloud foundation across infrastructure, containers, databases and testing, while Temenos continues to optimise its banking capabilities for increasingly diverse workloads.

As banking evolves, cloud-native architecture, modularity and AI will increasingly become interconnected parts of the same transformation journey.

Together, Temenos and Microsoft are helping build and test the foundations for the next generation of banking at scale.

Eli Lilly and Co (NYSE:LLY) said on Monday it will acquire privately held Merida Biosciences for up to $2.88 billion in cash, part of a deal-making push to broaden its treatments for immune-related and allergic diseases.

The acquisition continues a run of dealmaking for Lilly, whose deal spending this year has outpaced prior years as it looks to diversify beyond its blockbuster obesity and diabetes franchises.

The agreement includes an upfront payment and additional amounts tied to milestones, though Lilly did not disclose specific terms.

Merida is developing medicines that selectively target antibodies driving a range of immune-related conditions. Its lead candidate, MER511, is in early-stage development for autoimmune disorders including Graves' disease and thyroid eye disease. Lilly said initial data showed the drug substantially lowered thyroid-stimulating antibodies linked to those conditions, with a favorable early safety profile.

Graves' disease causes the thyroid to produce excess hormone, while thyroid eye disease can lead to inflammation, eye bulging, double vision and impaired vision. Current treatments include antithyroid medications, radioactive iodine and surgery, alongside two FDA-approved drugs for thyroid eye disease, Amgen's Tepezza and Viridian Therapeutics' Lumvoa.

Merida's pipeline also includes MER769, an experimental treatment for food allergy, asthma and other allergic diseases, along with earlier-stage programs targeting kidney and other immune-mediated conditions.

The deal is expected to close in the fourth quarter.

Shares of Lilly were down around 1.7% on Monday morning.

text:
NEW YORK, Aug 31 (Reuters) - Activist investor Elliott Investment Management has built a stake in Paris-based Air Liquide and is urging the French multinational company to improve its margins, sources familiar with the matter told Reuters.

Elliott has been engaging with the company for months and is urging management to make improvements to better compete with rivals in the industrial gases sector, the sources said. The exact size of Elliott's stake could not be immediately learned.

Elliott declined to comment, while Air Liquide did not respond to a request for comment.

Air Liquide has a market value of roughly EUR108 billion ($125.5 billion) and has two main competitors, Linde and Air Products and Chemicals.

Analysts say the margin gap between Air Liquide and Linde, which has a market value of $225 billion, has increased in recent years, suggesting that Linde's operational optimization plan has been successful while Air Liquide's leaves room for improvement.

As of mid-year 2026, Linde's operating margins were 30%, compared with Air Liquide's 21%, according to LSEG data. Analysts said that gap is expected to remain steady for several years. This would give Air Liquide management room to make improvements, industry analysts have said.

Linde repurchased $4.6 billion in shares in 2025. Air Liquide authorized buybacks last year but executed them in late February to early March of 2026, according to company filings, coming to EUR167 million ($193 million).

Air Liquide has an investor day scheduled for early October, and investors have said they hope management will reveal plans to improve margins and detail additional share buybacks.

Air Liquide also has an electronics division which provides gases to make AI chips, something some investors have called a growth engine hidden within the industrial gases business due to the ongoing AI infrastructure buildout.

Elliott, one of the world's biggest activist investors, has recently pushed for changes at the London Stock Exchange Group and chip design software giant Synopsys.

title: Why Delta Air Lines Quietly Killed 3 New York-JFK Routes & Sent Them All To LaGuardia Instead
authors: Louis Hardiman, Aaron Bailey, James Pearson
description:
After an initial suspension in summer 2026, Delta Air Lines has now permanently deleted its routes from John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) to Houston's George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH), Memphis' Frederick W. Smith International Airport (MEM), and St. Louis Lambert International Airport (STL).
Houston, Memphis, and St. Louis will now be connected to New York through LaGuardia Airport (LGA).
It's also notable that none of the routes were particularly popular while they were operating out of JFK.
In the years to come, it will be fascinating to see what other routes are pushed out to LaGuardia, and how that further cuts its significance in Delta's domestic operations.
JetBlue pushed into Delta's LaGuardia stronghold by engaging in a bidding war to obtain the 22 takeoff and landing slots that have become available at LaGuardia now that Spirit Airlines has ceased operations.
text:
After an initial suspension in summer 2026, Delta Air Lines has now permanently deleted its routes from John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) to Houston's George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH), Memphis' Frederick W. Smith International Airport (MEM), and St. Louis Lambert International Airport (STL). Each of these routes last operated on June 7, 2026, initially scheduled to begin in early September. Houston, Memphis, and St. Louis will now be connected to New York through LaGuardia Airport (LGA). "We apologize for any inconvenience this may cause and will contact affected customers directly to discuss alternative travel options,” said an airline spokesperson, as reported by AirlineGeeks.com. Simple Flying has contacted Delta for further comment.

Delta calls the move "routine network planning." It's all part of a broader formalization of the carrier's two-hub doctrine in New York. JFK will increasingly act as its hub for premium and intercontinental services. Meanwhile, LaGuardia will focus on domestic aviation, such as the carrier's flights to Houston, Memphis, and St. Louis.

How Have High Aviation Fuel Prices Created Incentives For The Change?

Aeronautics Magazine writes that the cost of aviation fuel has increased by up to 73%. It peaked at $4.17 per gallon. The result was Delta's quarterly fuel bill reaching an astonishing $2 billion. These costs have to be offset somewhere to ensure that the carrier can keep out of the red. One way is to fly less. “We are meaningfully reducing capacity in the current quarter with a downward bias until we see the fuel situation improve,” said Delta Chief Executive Officer Ed Bastian in April.

Another way for airlines to restructure their costs is to examine exactly how they are using expensive and restricted slots at the world's busiest airports, such as JFK. A tiny Embraer E175 or Bombardier CRJ-900 flying the 1,415-mile (2,280 km) route to Houston or 892-mile (1,435 km) route to St. Louis will use up a slot that could be used by a massive Airbus A350 flying to London or Paris. Such routes attract far more high-paying and premium passengers, generating a more robust margin. Rerouting to less restrictive and expensive airports is one solution. The carrier also told investors that it would target off-peak flying, such as through red-eye flights and edge-of-day departures.

It's also notable that none of the routes were particularly popular while they were operating out of JFK. Load factors were 81.9% for the Houston route, 81.3% for the Memphis route, and 67.1% to St. Louis. Frequencies may have needed to be cut if the carrier had stayed at JFK to offset the lower revenue across the entire aircraft caused by empty seats.

How Does Delta's Decision Benefit LaGuardia?

Delta maintains its connection to each of these three cities through its flights from LaGuardia. They operate at a frequency of four daily flights to Houston, three to Memphis, and four to St. Louis. Adding these services further consolidates LaGuardia's position as Delta's primary northeastern domestic hub. The third quarter will see 21,597 scheduled domestic services, making it Delta's fifth-largest base nationwide.

The table below shows the narrowbody aircraft currently operated by Delta. The number of these jets flying from LaGuardia will only increase as Delta leans more heavily into the hub for domestic aviation. It uses data from Planespotters.net:

Meanwhile, JFK will have just 14,740 during Q3 2026. In the years to come, it will be fascinating to see what other routes are pushed out to LaGuardia, and how that further cuts its significance in Delta's domestic operations. Further abandonment of JFK will also only help Delta's rival airlines that continue to provide a range of domestic services from the airport.

How Does The Move Help JetBlue?

With the JFK-Houston route dropped, JetBlue will now be the only hometown carrier that still flies the route nonstop. This is a substantial advance for JetBlue at a time when it is becoming increasingly adversarial to Delta. JetBlue pushed into Delta's LaGuardia stronghold by engaging in a bidding war to obtain the 22 takeoff and landing slots that have become available at LaGuardia now that Spirit Airlines has ceased operations. JetBlue won this fight on July 20. It offered $58.5 million for the slots, defeating Frontier Airlines, which had bid $57.5 million.

JetBlue will likely use these slots on routes directly competing with Delta. However, the exact way that this will materialize remains to be seen. “We’re currently evaluating how best to utilize these slots as we consider opportunities to bring more of JetBlue’s competitive, customer-focused service to New York. We expect any expansion at LGA related to these slots would start in 2027," said JetBlue.

The table below shows JetBlue's fleet according to the Planespotters.net:

The slots do come with some stipulations. For example, JetBlue will have to assume Spirit's lease of the Marine Air Terminal, Terminal A, when it wants to start using them.

How Does LaGuardia's Perimeter Rule Force Delta To Use It As A Domestic Fortress?

Since the 1950s, LaGuardia has had a unique 'perimeter rule'. It limits how far carriers can fly to and from the airport. When it was originally set, the perimeter had a radius of 2,000 miles (3,200 km) outward from LaGuardia. In the 1980s, this was restricted further to 1,500 miles (2,400 km). The rule prevents LaGuardia from becoming excessively crowded. It also ensures that JFK and Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) can maintain their statuses as New York City's main hubs for international and longer domestic flying.

A consequence of this rule is that it naturally angles LaGuardia towards being a short-haul domestic hub. Part of the reason that it has picked up its domestic status for Delta is that it just makes sense.

The table below shows the top ten busiest domestic routes from LaGuardia from June 2025 to May 2026, with the perimeter rule clearly having an effect:

There are some exceptions to the rule that allow for more expansive flying. In 1984, daily flights to Denver outside of the perimeter were allowed. The rule has also been scrapped for Saturdays. That is because Saturday is traditionally aviation's quietest day. As Delta shifts more services to LaGuardia, it will be interesting to see if it decides to use the Saturday exemption as a way to include slightly longer domestic flights in the strategy.

Which Other Services Is Delta Adding?

The moving of Delta's New York to Houston, St. Louis and Memphis to LaGuardia comes as part of Delta's broadening of its domestic network, which has had a focus on New York's third airport. Simple Flying's Victoria Agronsky recently reported on a new seasonal service to Melbourne Orlando International Airport (MLB) this winter. Passengers will be able to use these flights to get out of New York's bitter winters for some time in the Floridian sun. Delta will have two flights a week to Melbourne Orlando, holding them on Saturdays and Sundays. They will start on December 19 and finish on May 2, 2027. An Embraer E175 will be used.

Delta is also expanding its services from LaGuardia into the international market. An example is the route from LaGuardia to Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport (BDA). These routes will be operated four times a week using A319 jets. Delta has operated this route before, in 2007 and from 2013 to 2014. The route is particularly notable in the context of this article because the airline is replacing flights from JFK. Despite being an international flight, the hop over to the Atlantic island is well within the 1,500-mile perimeter. Therefore, the flights can be executed on any day that Delta chooses. Passengers will be able to access this route from October 6, with the service from JFK being discontinued the day before.

Premium seats will be available on the A319s executing the LaGuardia to Bermuda route. They will offer 12 Delta First, 24 Delta Comfort, and 96 Delta Main seats.

description:

text:
Apple today submitted new evidence in its lawsuit against OpenAI, with the hope that the new information will persuade the judge to grant an expedited discovery process.

Apple filed a theft of trade secrets lawsuit against OpenAI employees Chang Liu and Tang Tan in July, accusing them of using multiple methods to steal data from Apple. Liu kept an Apple-issued MacBook after he left for OpenAI, and Apple got it back after the lawsuit was filed. Apple now says forensic analysis of the laptop has uncovered more evidence of Liu's use of Apple information and his attempts to hide what he'd done.

From the lawsuit:

Mr. Liu not only downloaded a confidential Apple circuit schematic but also used it in his work at OpenAI;

Far from his unauthorized access to Apple's third-party cloud storage being unknown to him, Mr. Liu and others at OpenAI were well-aware of that access;

Mr. Liu, upon learning of Apple's internal investigation of him, sent instructions for destroying evidence to an OpenAI colleague who confirmed she would comply; and

Mr. Liu used a tool in his work at OpenAI that has the same name as an internal Apple engineering application used for Apple development work.

Liu downloaded the circuit schematic from Apple in March, two months after he left the company. Liu used the schematic to run a simulation using electrical engineering tool LTspice, and then messaged people telling them he ran the simulation for power conversion development work. Liu described how he trained an AI agent to run LTspice.

According to the filing, he said he was "[f]eeling AI all day long," and that "[i]n the past hour," his AI "agent learned how to run LTspice, look at result, tune compensation parameter." "I try to make a behavior buck," he wrote. "With voltage outer and current inner. Everything ideal. It still took me a day.. now it's two hour. Including learning fresh."

"Oh man! Why do they even need you then?" the person Liu was talking to reportedly replied.

Liu used the Apple schematic on a Mac mini that later synced to the MacBook he took from Apple, which is why Apple knows about it. Apple now wants to investigate the ‌Mac mini‌ and other devices Liu still has in his possession.

Apple says the "shocking evidence" is proof that its trade secrets are in active use and evidence is being destroyed, which is why expedited discovery is needed.

Apple initially asked for expedited discovery earlier this month, also requesting an injunction preventing OpenAI from using its trade secrets. OpenAI responded by asking the court to dismiss the lawsuit, claiming the accusations were "meritless." OpenAI also published a public statement calling the lawsuit "careless, aggressive and oddly personal" and stating that it does not "have, nor want, any of their trade secrets" because it is "much more interested in building innovative products and technologies that push the frontier."

Judge Edward J. Davila is set to hear arguments in the case on October 1.

Officially announced in Paris during the French-Saudi strategic partnership council, this major agreement provides for the development of a portfolio of over 4,000 keys in the Kingdom. This major project forms part of a drive to structure accommodation capacity to meet the growing influx of religious and business tourism.

This announcement marks a major milestone in French-Saudi economic relations, illustrating the strength of bilateral tourism investment. The French-Saudi strategic partnership council serves as a high-level springboard for such intercontinental cooperation. By choosing Paris to formalise this project, Accor and Al Qimmah Hospitality highlight the international reach of their collaboration. This long-term alliance aims to introduce global operational standards into a dynamic, rapidly restructuring market.

Novotel Makkah, a new 850-key giant

The upcoming property under the Novotel brand will feature a major capacity of 850 rooms, making it one of the flagship projects in Accor’s regional portfolio. The Novotel brand is internationally recognised for its positioning focused on modernity, comfort and welcoming hospitality, qualities particularly suited to the expectations of a diverse clientele of pilgrims and business travellers.

Designing an 850-key hotel requires considerable architectural and operational expertise. The infrastructure is conceived to handle large visitor flows while maintaining smooth, high-quality service during peak periods, which are frequent in the holy cities. The focus will be on versatile, modular living spaces, providing guests with reliable, functional accommodation that is seamlessly integrated into local dynamics.

Hospitality dynamics in the holy cities

The accommodation market in Makkah and Madinah is characterised by continuous structural demand and extraordinary peak visitor numbers linked to the spiritual calendar. Welcoming millions of pilgrims each year imposes operational demands on hotel infrastructure that are unique in the world, requiring rigorous management of logistics, security and services.

The increased presence of global hotel operators helps standardise service offerings and bring the expertise required to manage these massive flows. This shift towards professionalisation in the sector meets the rising quality expectations of international visitors. International brands, through their brand awareness, provide reassuring benchmarks of comfort and service quality, thereby consolidating the destination’s reputation on the global stage.

A major new address on the 2030 horizon

Scheduled to open its doors by 2030, the upcoming Novotel-branded property promises to be a cornerstone of hospitality in the holy city. With an 850-room capacity for the future Novotel, the establishment will significantly reinforce the hotel group’s footprint in major religious tourism destinations, addressing growing demand from pilgrims for high-quality stays across various price points. This project consolidates Accor’s status as the leading international hotel operator in the region, while extending midscale comfort standards into the heart of the holy cities.

Achieving the 2030 targets reflects the meticulous planning required to successfully deliver major construction projects of this scale. By working closely with Al Qimmah Hospitality, the French group ensures a rollout rooted in local market realities while maintaining brand identity. This future location thus positions itself as a modern answer to the demands of a rapidly transforming market.

A global partnership passing the 4,000-room milestone

This new signing is not an isolated event, but a direct continuation of the master development agreement signed in 2025 between the two partners. The joint portfolio now extends across multiple strategic properties representing over 4,000 keys located in key hubs across the country: Jeddah, Makkah and Madinah. Across the Mercure Makkah Shesha, ibis Styles Makkah Mesfalah, Mövenpick Madinah, Swissôtel Jeddah and now Novotel Makkah brands, the alliance spans a broad spectrum of hotel segments, from economy to premium, catering to all guest profiles.

This multi-brand strategy is designed to cater to the diverse visitor profiles travelling through the region. Whether for budget stays or high-end services, the deployed brands allow for a complementary offering. The geographical distribution between the major gateway of Jeddah and the holy cities of Makkah and Madinah creates a unified, cohesive accommodation ecosystem dedicated to the guest experience.

Accor’s expansion in Saudi Arabia by 2030

Accor’s ongoing expansion reflects a lasting strategic commitment to the Saudi market. By establishing its key brands in the country’s most dynamic economic and cultural hubs, the group is actively responding to the sector’s restructuring. This footprint is accompanied by the digitisation of services and the enhancement of global loyalty programmes, aimed at building loyalty among domestic and international business and leisure guests seeking modern standards.

A project in line with Saudi Vision 2030 ambitions

Accor’s expansion aligns seamlessly with the macroeconomic objectives set by the Saudi authorities. By strategically expanding its hotel infrastructure, the group directly contributes to the diversification ambitions of the Saudi economy driven by the Saudi Vision 2030 plan. This state agenda aims to dramatically increase capacity for pilgrims and international tourists, requiring a rapid upgrade in national accommodation offerings and meticulous structuring of the regional tourism landscape.

To support these ambitions, modernising public infrastructure is essential, particularly through transport network developments and urban regeneration in historic centres. The involvement of major global operators like Accor adds clear value to this transition, enhancing the country’s international profile while building a sustainable tourism model aligned with government objectives.

Tamayyaz, the human catalyst to train local talent

Developing local skills represents a key challenge for the future of Saudi hospitality. Through the Tamayyaz by Accor initiative, the group offers comprehensive training pathways designed to prepare future national hospitality leaders. This scheme focuses on integrating young talent across all areas of operations, from daily management to strategic leadership, driving long-term skill enhancement within the local workforce.

Training local talent at the heart of the partnership

Beyond building physical infrastructure, the alliance strategy places paramount importance on human capital and job nationalisation. Leveraging the national Tamayyaz by Accor training programme, rolled out in close collaboration with the Saudi Ministry of Tourism, the hotel group is actively engaged in vocational education. The initiative has set a goal to train and recruit over 3,000 Saudi nationals by 2030, thereby shaping the next generation of hospitality executives within the Kingdom.

This institutional collaboration strengthens the programme’s relevance by aligning it directly with actual industry needs. By offering rewarding career prospects, the project contributes to the emergence of a modern, attractive service economy for younger Saudi generations. The involvement of Accor teams ensures world-class skills transfer, guaranteeing long-term excellence in hospitality across future establishments.

name: Microsoft
title: AWS and Microsoft Azure collaborate to expand multicloud networking
description:
Starting today, customers can provision private, high-speed connectivity between Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Microsoft Azure on demand through AWS Interconnect – multicloud.
With Azure connectivity now in Public Preview, AWS Interconnect – multicloud spans all three non-AWS major cloud service providers (CSPs) – Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure – giving customers the same simplified, on-demand networking experience between AWS and other CSPs.
Continuing the multicloud journey AWS introduced AWS Interconnect – multicloud in preview at re:Invent 2025, publishing an open API specification for network interoperability that raised the bar for the industry and established a framework any provider can adopt, inviting the broader industry to participate.
Throughout that journey, customers consistently asked us: “When can we connect to Microsoft Azure?” Today’s announcement answers that call and brings the AWS Interconnect – multicloud story full circle.
With AWS and Azure now connected through AWS Interconnect – multicloud, customers get unified management, accelerated innovation, reduced risk, and future-proof architecture.
text:
As organizations embrace multicloud strategies at an accelerating pace, the ability to move workloads seamlessly between cloud providers has become essential. Yet establishing resilient, high-performance private connectivity between clouds has historically required customers to navigate complex and diverse physical infrastructure, multiple connectivity providers, and invest weeks or months of manual provisioning.

Starting today, customers can provision private, high-speed connectivity between Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Microsoft Azure on demand through AWS Interconnect – multicloud. With Azure connectivity now in Public Preview, AWS Interconnect – multicloud spans all three non-AWS major cloud service providers (CSPs) – Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure – giving customers the same simplified, on-demand networking experience between AWS and other CSPs.

Continuing the multicloud journey

AWS introduced AWS Interconnect – multicloud in preview at re:Invent 2025, publishing an open API specification for network interoperability that raised the bar for the industry and established a framework any provider can adopt, inviting the broader industry to participate. Any cloud provider willing to meet the requirements can join. Since then, AWS has collaborated with other major CSPs to bring this vision to life. Throughout that journey, customers consistently asked us: “When can we connect to Microsoft Azure?”

Today’s announcement answers that call and brings the AWS Interconnect – multicloud story full circle. Customers who operate between AWS and Azure can now manage their connectivity through a single, managed experience, without compromise.

“Customers told us they wanted a better way to connect workloads spanning AWS and Azure, and the old ways of doing it were clunky. With AWS Interconnect-multicloud and Azure Multicloud Interconnect, we’re proving what’s possible when both sides commit to a high bar: MACsec security out of the box, four-nines availability, and scalability at the click of a button.”

– Robert Kennedy, VP of Network Services at AWS

A consistent experience across every cloud

The AWS-Azure connectivity experience is built on the same principles that have guided every collaboration under AWS Interconnect – multicloud.

Provisioning happens in a few clicks, versus taking weeks or months. Customers get dedicated, private bandwidth between AWS and Azure on demand—no physical infrastructure to manage and no circuit cabling to wait for. The experience is cloud-native simple: establish managed connectivity directly from the AWS Management Console or CLI and the Azure portal.

High resiliency is built in by design. A quad-redundant architecture across physically diverse interconnect facilities and routers ensures enterprise-grade availability. When a customer creates a new Interconnect, AWS and the other CSP provision four independent logical paths. A router can go down for maintenance, two additional independent disruptions can occur simultaneously, and the customer’s traffic continues uninterrupted. Even a full site loss doesn’t impact service because the remaining site carries the traffic.

Security is always priority 0 at AWS. MACsec encryption between edge routers protects data in transit from the moment it leaves one CSP’s network and arrives at the other. This is non-negotiable. Any CSP that cannot meet the security and availability bar does not get connected.

“Organizations are increasingly building applications, data platforms, and AI solutions that span multiple cloud environments. This collaboration between Microsoft and AWS helps simplify how customers connect those environments, helping to provide secure, high-performance networking with less operational complexity. By making multicloud connectivity easier and more accessible, we are giving customers greater flexibility to innovate on their own terms while accelerating their digital and AI transformation journeys.”

– Narayan Annamalai, Vice President, Product Management, Azure Networking, Microsoft

Why it matters for customers

Enterprises increasingly deploy workloads where they run best and at AWS, we design our services to give customers the freedom to choose technology that best suits their needs. However, multicloud is often less about choosing the ideal tool for each job and more about how businesses actually evolve. Companies acquire other companies and end up with applications spanning different cloud providers. Independent Software Vendors (ISVs) need to deploy solutions across whichever environment their customers use. Regulatory requirements dictate the need to deploy applications to more than one cloud. Until the launch of AWS Interconnect-multicloud, organizations relied on complex interconnections, multiple third-party networking arrangements, or the public internet to stitch things together. With AWS and Azure now connected through AWS Interconnect – multicloud, customers get unified management, accelerated innovation, reduced risk, and future-proof architecture.

A single connectivity model reduces operational overhead and training costs, giving teams unified management without juggling disparate tooling. That operational simplicity translates directly into accelerated innovation, with engineers spending less time wiring networks and more time building products.

Risk also drops. Consistent security posture, monitoring, and SLAs across every cloud-to-cloud link mean fewer blind spots. AWS Interconnect includes Network Synthetic Monitor at no additional cost. When it detects packet loss, it triangulates whether the issue originates on the AWS side and tells the customer where the problem lives, eliminating the ambiguity of troubleshooting across cloud environments.

Finally, the architecture is future-proof. The open specification means new providers can join without requiring customers to re-architect.

What’s next

Together, AWS and Microsoft will continue to expand regional availability, increase bandwidth options, and deepen the experience based on customer feedback. The ambition extends beyond cloud-to-cloud. AWS aims to shift the paradigm on all connectivity. The goal is a world where customers can turn up a global network and connect to anything they want with a few simple clicks. The open specification remains available for additional providers who share our vision of simplified, interoperable cloud connectivity.

description:
On August 31, Adobe (NASDAQ:ADBE) committed more than $4 billion to giving away its AI tools.
The deal includes a new image generation model tuned for Saudi culture, letting users create images from Arabic-language prompts.
It is a striking bet for a stock that trades like the market expects its growth to stall.
A Business Where AI Is Adding, Not Subtracting That confidence has some backing.
The fear is straightforward: generative AI now lets anyone produce images and design work without needing Photoshop expertise, a skill that used to be the whole point of buying Adobe's software.
text:
On August 31, Adobe (NASDAQ:ADBE) committed more than $4 billion to giving away its AI tools. The company will offer 12 months of free access to its Firefly Standard subscription and Adobe Express Premium features to more than 27 million eligible citizens and residents in Saudi Arabia, expanding its partnership with the country's Ministry of Communications and Information Technology and the government-backed AI firm Humain. The deal includes a new image generation model tuned for Saudi culture, letting users create images from Arabic-language prompts. It is a striking bet for a stock that trades like the market expects its growth to stall.

A Business Where AI Is Adding, Not Subtracting

That confidence has some backing. Adobe's AI-first products, the newer tools built around generative features, saw their annualized recurring revenue triple year over year to more than $500 million, evidence that artificial intelligence is adding to Adobe's business rather than just threatening it. The Saudi Arabia expansion extends that momentum internationally, giving Firefly and Express a built-in user base of millions who might otherwise never try Adobe's software, in a region where Humain and the country's sovereign wealth fund are pouring money into localized AI development.

The core business is not showing cracks either. Adobe's most recent quarter delivered $6.62 billion in revenue, up 13% year over year and a company record, extending two years of consistent low double-digit growth. Subscriptions make up virtually all of that revenue, and Adobe closed the quarter holding $27.1 billion of annualized recurring revenue, plus another $22.3 billion in contracted revenue still to be recognized, a backlog that gives management visibility most software companies would envy. Net margin for fiscal 2025 came in near 30%, and free cash flow neared $9.9 billion for the year, funding both new deals like the Semrush acquisition and buybacks that retired about 2% of shares outstanding in just three months.

A Valuation That Still Smells Doubt

Yet the stock's roughly 10 times forward earnings multiple says the market is not convinced the good times continue. The fear is straightforward: generative AI now lets anyone produce images and design work without needing Photoshop expertise, a skill that used to be the whole point of buying Adobe's software. Adobe faces that pressure not just from AI-focused startups but from Microsoft, and any regulatory shift like the European Union's AI Act could raise compliance costs and complicate how Adobe trains its own models.
